articles.headline: The Church, and the Moral and Social Condition of Our People
articles.author: Progress
articles.summary: It is humiliating that the greatest amount of vice and misery among our people exists in the vicinity of our churches. This is attributable to the fact, that that part of the city has stood for years in an unimproved condition. The houses, old and untenantable, have been deserted long since by respectable people, and are now rented out by rooms at an enormous rent. [Goes on to the rum shops, the landlords, tavern keepers and police officers, 'of which latter there are no less than ten in the vicinity of Sixth and Lombard streets alone', and asks each church to appoint a committee of one or two to remonstrate.]

articles.summary: When I received my appointment in Baltimore City, on the 24th of April, from the hand of our beloved Bishop D. A. Payne... Quarterly meetings at Chambersburg, Greencastle and Mercersburg with Rev. William Waters, presiding elder; a watch presented to the pastor by Mr. Samuel Richardson, called on Rev. Terry Hollems [VERIFY] to present it. Out of the Philadelphia area: names not linked.

articles.headline: Welcome to our Colored Soldiers (editorial)
articles.summary: The good people of Pennsylvania, ever ready to show their appreciation of every good and noble act, have, through the Garnet E. R. League, of Harrisburg, made most brilliant arrangements to tender a formal welcome to our returned heroes. This reception will occur on next Tuesday, 14th inst., at Harrisburg. Recommends the Philadelphia and Reading Rail Road.

articles.headline: Life Insurance (editorial)
articles.summary: We are pleased to note the growing tendency among our people to have some of their spare means invested in paying for a policy of insurance upon their lives. Names the Security Life Insurance Company, which has lately paid a $2000 policy on the death of one of our citizens, well-known and much respected; the agent, Mr. Willets, has his office at 528 Walnut St., above 5th.

articles.headline: Decease of an Esteemed Member of Society (Maurice Hall)
articles.summary: We are called upon to make the painful announcement of the demise of our esteemed friend and fellow-townsman, Maurice Hall. He was taken ill on the 1st instant and died on the 8th instant, at a quarter after eleven o'clock. Bethel church has lost one of her brightest Christian ornaments; Brother Hall was one of the oldest, if not the oldest, member of Bethel church. He was between 73 and 75. Thus two of the most worthy of our citizens, Joshua Brown and Maurice Hall, have left us within the short space of forty-eight hours.
people: deceased Nov. 8, 1865; one of the oldest members of Bethel church, aged between 73 and 75
deceased within forty-eight hours of Maurice Hall (c. Nov. 6-8, 1865)

articles.headline: Notice to the Itinerant Ministers of the Philadelphia Annual Conference (superannuated preachers)
articles.author: A. W. Wayman
articles.summary: Dear Brethren: Allow me to call your attention to the collections ordered by the Annual Conference, for the superannuated preachers. There are two Reverend Fathers dependent on these collections for support. Rev. Jeremiah G. Bulah [VERIFY] is nearly a hundred years of age, and is very feeble.

articles.headline: Notice of a special meeting of the Pennsylvania State Equal Rights League
articles.author: William Nesbit
articles.summary: A special meeting of the Pennsylvania State Equal Rights League will be held in Harrisburg, on Monday evening, Nov. 13th; also a public meeting on the evening of the 14th, to lay the claims of the Equal Rights movement before the people of Pennsylvania. By order of the Executive Board, William Nesbit, Pres.; Jacob C. White, Charles B. Colly, Secretaries. Philadelphia, Nov. 7th, 1865.
people: secretary, Pennsylvania State Equal Rights League (printed 'Jacob C. White', no Jr./Sr.)

articles.headline: Obituary (George R. Todd)
articles.author: F. J. C.
articles.summary: Departed this life Oct. 31st, 1865, George [VERIFY] R. Todd, in the hope of a glorious immortality, aged 36 years, 8 months and 23 days. He had been in the naval service of the United States (ship Hartford), was sent home to Philadelphia, and subsequently removed to Wilmington to his mother's. Funeral sermon by Rev. Edward Chippy and Rev. Isaac Parker in the African Union Church; interred in St. Peter's cemetery.

articles.headline: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Pennsylvania State Equal Rights' League, held in Harrisburg, August 9th and 10th, 1865 (continued)
articles.author: J. C. White, Jr.
articles.summary: Continued from our issue of Sept. 2d. Morning Session, August 10. The League met at 10 o'clock, Mr. President Peck in the chair. The meeting was opened by the reading of the 86th Psalm, after which the roll was called and tax collected. Includes the Report of the Executive Board (signed J. C. White, Jr., Secretary), the list of auxiliary associations, the treasurers' accounts and the resolutions.
people: Secretary, Executive Board (printed 'J. C. White, Jr.')

articles.headline: The Funeral of the Late Maurice Hall
articles.summary: The funeral of our late much lamented brother, Maurice Hall, took place on last Monday, 13th inst., from his residence, No. 1043 Lombard street at 10 o'clock, A.M. The solemn cortege formed in the following order: official members of Bethel Church, Rev. Wm. Moore, pastor of do., the invited clergy, relatives of the deceased, followed by a vast concourse of friends.
people: deceased; residence No. 1043 Lombard street; leader and steward of Bethel; leading spirit in establishing the Aged Home

articles.headline: The Harrisburg Celebration
articles.summary: The city of Harrisburg was thronged on Tuesday with hosts of visitors from all parts of the State, all desirous of expressing in a proper manner the thanks of the people to the colored soldiers. The weather was fine. At 9 o'clock the military and civic societies assembled on State street, and the line having been formed, by 10 o'clock it was in motion.
people: evening speaker at the Wesleyan Union Church (printed 'J. C. White, Jr.' = Jacob C. White Jr.)
evening speaker at the Wesleyan Union Church

articles.headline: A Voice from Ashmun
articles.author: Inveritas [VERIFY]
articles.summary: It has been some time since I have communicated to the people through your columns. I now take this opportunity of informing the many friends of Ashmun how we are progressing here. The students have organized a literary society, called the 'Garnet Lyceum,' in honor of Henry Highland Garnet. Ashmun Institute, Oxford, Pa., Nov. 11th, 1865.

articles.headline: A Revival (First Colored Wesley Church, Lombard St.)
articles.author: I. H.
articles.summary: There being such a glorious revival going on at the First Colored Wesley Church, Lombard St., among the young folks especially, I thought it would be interesting to your readers. It has been in session now for four weeks, and between eighty and ninety, during that time, have declared that Jesus has opened their eyes. The meeting is still going on under the pastoral charge of the Rev. J. P. Hemmer [VERIFY].

articles.headline: Notice: Supreme Grand Tent of J. R. Giddings and Jolliffe Union
articles.summary: To whom it may concern. To perpetuate the names of two eminent statesmen, advocates of universal freedom and the rights of mankind, the several Tents of J. R. Giddings and Jolliffe Union met in solemn convention on the 11th day of March, 1865, in the city of Philadelphia, Pa. The Grand Body was organized under the name and title of the Supreme Grand Tent of J. R. Giddings and Jolliffe Union of the United States of North America.

articles.headline: Notice to our Citizens (Wm. Henry Williams seeks his aunt)
articles.summary: If this should meet the eye of Mrs. Henrietta Williams, formerly of Macon, Ga., or of any one who knows her address, a favor will be conferred by sending the same to her nephew Wm. Henry Williams, alias Ross, care of Christian Recorder, 619 Pine street. Nov 18-2t.

articles.headline: Obituary: Bethel Official Board on Maurice Hall; deaths
articles.summary: Philada., Nov. 12th, 1865. At a called meeting of the Official Board of Bethel A.M.E. Church, Sixth St. above Lombard, the Rev. Wm. Moore, elder in charge, presiding, to take action in relation to the death of Maurice Hall, late leader and steward in this church, preamble and resolutions were submitted by Bro. Henry Gordon and unanimously adopted. Died, in this city, on the 4th of Nov., Morris O. Connie [VERIFY], Sergt. Co. C., 41st Regt. U.S.C.T., aged 23 years, 10 months and 20 days. (In Newark, N.J., Oct. 15, Sister Nancy Scott, aged 81.)

articles.headline: A Visit to Wilmington, Del.
articles.author: N. H. Turpin
articles.summary: On the 15th of October last, I made a visit to Wilmington, my native place, the first time in sixteen years, to assist the Rev. D. P. Seaton with his quarterly meeting. It is astonishing to see the rapid progress the A.M.E. Church has made in that city within twenty years. Bishop A. W. Wayman preached on the fifth and left on the sixth for the City of Brotherly Love. Salem, N.J., Nov. 14th, 1865.

articles.headline: At Home (editor's return)
articles.summary: We give notice to our friends and the public that we have arrived home safe and sound, and for which we render thanks to a wise and protecting Creator. We are now ready to attend to any deferred business. We also call special attention of our Church and brethren to Bishop Payne's very interesting letter relative to the centenary.

articles.headline: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Pennsylvania State Equal Rights' League, Harrisburg, Aug. 9th and 10th, 1865 (continued)
articles.summary: [Continued from our last issue.] A communication was received from the Lewistown League. Mr. Bustill of Philadelphia objected to the reading of it. Mr. Forten, of Philadelphia, moved that the rules be suspended in order to consider an important resolution concerning the Ladies' Union Association. (Carried.)

articles.headline: Semi-Centenary of the A.M. Episcopal Church
articles.author: D. A. Payne
articles.summary: Mr. Editor: The majority of your readers who are members of the A.M.E. Church seem not to be aware of the interesting fact, that the 18th of next April fills up the first half century of our existence as an ecclesiastical establishment. Central Committee: Rev. J. M. Brown, D. W. Moore, Benj. T. Tanner, M. F. Sluby, J. A. Handy, S. L. Hammonds, J. J. Herbert. Goal $100,000 for Wilberforce University, Missions and the Book Concern.

articles.headline: Death of Dr. J. McCune Smith; Bishop Campbell's Visits; Missouri and Louisiana Conference Appointments
articles.summary: With heart almost too full for utterance do we attempt to apprise those of our readers who are not already acquainted with the fact, of the death of our distinguished fellow-worker, Dr. James McCune Smith. He breathed his last on Friday, the 17th inst., at his home in Williamsburgh, N.Y. (New York; out of scope.) Bishop J. P. Campbell is returning from the Missouri and Louisiana Conferences.
people: Bishop; returning from the Missouri and Louisiana Conferences

articles.headline: Tribute of Respect: Bethel Sabbath School teachers on Maurice Hall
articles.summary: At a special meeting of the teachers of Bethel Sabbath School, held for the purpose of taking action in relation to the sudden demise of Maurice Hall, presided over by the Superintendent, L. R. Seymour, the following preamble and resolutions were submitted and adopted: Whereas, we have learned with deep regret of the sudden demise of Maurice Hall, one of the founders of our school. Nov. 12, 1865.
people: deceased; one of the founders of the Bethel Sabbath School; left an aged widow and only son

articles.headline: Letter from Salem (N.J.)
articles.author: Joseph Gibbs [VERIFY]
articles.summary: Mr. Editor: Again I resume my pen to note a few of the passing events, as times are lively, and the wheel of improvement continues to move slowly in our midst. On Sabbath, the 5th inst., our hearts were made to rejoice with the presence of our highly esteemed Bishop, the Right Rev. A. W. Wayman. This is the first year Salem has been set apart as a station; N. H. Turpin is the first pastor. Hon. Wm. Steward, of Bridgeton, came en route for Trenton to meet the executive committee of the Equal Rights League of the State of New Jersey. Salem, Nov. 6th, 1865.

articles.headline: Cheating the Soldiers. A Warning.
articles.summary: We wish to call the special attention of our soldiers that are now being mustered out and paid off at Camp Cadwallader, to the fact that there are a certain party of vending Jews who frequent the locality with their wagons, for the purpose of decoying and swindling the unwary. Recommends Mr. E. Matlack & Son, 904 Market St., or Jones' one-price establishment.

articles.headline: Bishops' Meeting; Half a Centenary of the A.M.E. Church; A New Masonic Gavel; Agents
articles.summary: We are truly glad that our Bishops are going to have a meeting, about the 17th of this month. A New Masonic Gavel: a monthly paper published at Annapolis, Md., called the Masonic Gavel, devoted exclusively to the cause of Free Masonry, edited and published by a colored gentleman named John W. Reams. Agents named for New Orleans, Mobile and Natchez (out of scope).

articles.headline: Equal Rights (letter on the Philadelphia leagues)
articles.author: J. W. Brown
articles.summary: Mr. Editor: As this seems to be the time for agitation, and as our people in Philadelphia appear to be at a stand still in reference to their equal rights, I wish to make a few timely suggestions. There are in this city a number of Equal Rights' Leagues, supported by the few for the direct interest and benefit of the masses. There are meetings held time after time, and there is scarcely enough at these meetings to form a quorum.

articles.headline: Letter from Woodbury, N.J. (Freedmen's Relief Association)
articles.author: Lucy Ann Tudas [VERIFY]
articles.summary: I will commence by giving a brief account of a public demonstration, held in the A.M.E. church of this place, on the evening of the 23d inst., for the benefit of the Freedmen's Relief Association, which society was organized a few months ago, under the direction of the ladies. Address by Rev. N. H. Turpin, from Salem; $32.01 [VERIFY] realized.

articles.headline: A Donation Visit (Fair Haven, N.J.)
articles.author: M. Lee, R. Coates [VERIFY], M. Brown, Committee
articles.summary: Fair Haven, N.J., Nov. 17, 1865. We feel it our duty to return thanks to God and to the friends in general for what they have done for us. We were back with preacher's salary, and through the exertion of three sisters attached to our church, we were enabled to raise the sum of thirty-five dollars, which we shall pay to our worthy pastor, Rev. J. H. Jones.

articles.headline: Car Question Settled in Cincinnati (editorial note and report)
articles.summary: We give place this week to a righteous decision given by Judge Storer, in favor of a colored man, $800. Colored people can now ride in any car they choose, just as Philadelphia rail companies will have yet to come to, and it would be much better for them to come to it at once than to be driven by law. Report of Isaac Young vs. the Passenger Street Railroad Company (Cincinnati) follows, continued on page 2, column 1 (jury verdict $800).

articles.headline: Notice: Boling and Houston no longer employed by the Book Concern
articles.summary: Our two young friends, Thomas H. Boling and C. J. Houston, are no longer in the employ of the A. M. E. Book Concern. May success attend them in the business they propose to carry on. ED.

articles.summary: Unknown persons, pretending to be agents for this paper, are sneaking around this city collecting money; one went into an eating saloon and collected money for an advertisement. No names given.

articles.headline: Letter from Camp Cadwalader
articles.author: Jacob S. Johnson
articles.summary: By special request we publish the following letter for its own merit: Camp Cadwalader, Phila., Pa., December 2d, 1865. Mr. Editor: Allow me, through the medium of your valuable sheet, to return my heartfelt thanks to the officers of the 25th United States Colored Infantry, for the kindness they extended to me, while a member of Co. H. Thanks Colonel F. L. Hitchcock, Lieut. Col. J. W. H. Reisinger, Captain A. A. Shattuck (Co. articles.headline: Gone Up Another Step (Banneker delegates admitted to the Literary Societies' convention)
articles.summary: The Literary Societies of Philadelphia met in convention on Monday night, the 4th inst., to which colored delegates, from the Banneker Association, were duly accredited. After a powerful address from our esteemed friend, Mr. O. V. Cato, one of the teachers of the High School for colored youth, they were admitted to seats in the Society. Onward still, moves the world.

articles.headline: Letter from Morristown, N.J.: Dedication of Bethel Church
articles.author: W. H. W. Winder
articles.summary: Mr. Editor: After a long silence I again essay to write a few lines for your valuable paper ... After being transferred from the Philadelphia District to the New York District, I received an appointment, in June last, from Bishop A. W. Wayman, to the Morristown station. The church was enlarged by colored carpenters (Gabriel McGill of Stanhope, N.J., his son Henry A. McGill, and John A. Solomon; a well dug by James F. Hoy) and dedicated on Sabbath, November 26th, by the Rev. Wm. Moore, of Bethel Church, Philadelphia, who organized the society over twenty years ago; Rev. Joseph Benedict assisted; Brother Henry Ader welcomed them. Dated Morristown, N.J., Dec. 4, 1865.
people: pastor, Bethel Church, Philadelphia (Rev.); dedicated the church

articles.headline: A Surprise (St. Thomas' Church Parsonage)

articles.summary: On the evening of the 30th ult., at about half past eight o'clock, there was a gentle ring at the door-bell of St. Thomas' Church Parsonage, which we hastened to answer, and were greeted with a dozen or more smiling countenances, who were ushered into the parlor, each bearing a basket or attractive package. A purse of twenty-five dollars was placed in Mrs. Alston's hand. 'We cannot refrain from revealing that of the leader of them, viz: Mrs. James H. George.' Philadelphia, Dec. 4th, 1865.

articles.headline: Appeal of the Trustees of the African Methodist Episcopal Book Concern, of Philadelphia (purchase of No. 631 Pine Street)
articles.author: Elisha Weaver
articles.summary: To the Bishops and Ministers of the several Districts of the African Methodist Episcopal Church of America: Dear Brethren: It affords us pleasure to inform you, that after nearly fifty years of the organization of our beloved Church, we have at last succeeded in purchasing a house and lot, in a good location, for our Book Concern and paper, No. 631 Pine street, Philadelphia, not far from where we are now doing business. We have borrowed money to make the first payment, and will get possession on the first of March, 1866. Brethren, we want the sum of $4,000 by the 25th of April, 1866 ...

articles.headline: At Church Last Sabbath (Wesley and Bethel, Dec. 10; returned soldiers; Bethel choir)
articles.summary: On last Sabbath morning we attended divine service at Wesley Church, of which Rev. Jacob Mitchell is pastor, and heard our young brother from California, Rev. John Jenifer. ... At three o'clock we attended Bethel Church to hear Elder Moore's address to the returned soldiers. The church was crowded to its utmost capacity, both up and down stairs. ... After he had concluded, Rev. Jacob Mitchell followed in an exhortation. ... We never heard Bethel choir perform so well as they did on this occasion.

articles.headline: Death of Mrs. Julia C. Collins
articles.summary: We are sorry to inform our readers that we have received a letter from Mr. S. C. Collins, informing us of the death of his estimable wife, Mrs. Julia C. Collins, authoress of 'The Curse of Caste; or, the Slave Bride.' She departed this life on the 25th of November last, and, as the letter says, in the full triumph of everlasting bliss. ... deprived of the pleasure of reading the balance of the beautiful story which she was writing for our paper.

articles.headline: Bishop's Council
articles.summary: On Monday, the 18th, our Bishops will meet, in this city. We anticipate a good time. This is as it ought to be and we hope that they will all meet, if life and health will permit them.

articles.headline: A Letter from Harrisburg (arrest of two discharged colored soldiers)
articles.author: James Robison; James W. Loney
articles.summary: On Thursday afternoon, December 5th, James Robinson, of the Third Regiment, who has just been discharged like myself, was walking along the street, when a small boy, about nine years old, came up and insulted us. Mr. Robinson said to him, 'Go home, you young scamp.' Just then came several officers of the city, and we were arrested and put in the lock-up. We were treated very badly ... Mr. Barrmot [VERIFY], the chief of Police, said to me, 'You are insulted, are you? Who are you to be insulted? You are nothing but a nigger.' ... 'What's your name, sir?' 'James W. Loney.' 'Where are you from, sir?' 'Philadelphia.' Harrisburg, Dec. 5th, 1865.
people: discharged colored soldier, of Philadelphia; arrested at Harrisburg; co-signer

articles.author: Nicodemus
articles.summary: Signed 'Nicodemus', Philada., Dec. 10th, 1865. articles.headline: Letter from Wilmington, Del.: concert by a Philadelphia company (conclusion)
articles.author: D. P. Seaton
articles.summary: (Begun on p. 1, col. 7, 'The Ball is Still Moving.') Our citizens immediately commenced to prepare for the concert, and at the hour of six o'clock they commenced to stream towards the appointed place ... Black and white, rich and poor, old and young, met together on this occasion ... The concert was conducted splendidly ... Mrs. Merthe Collins acted as leader upon the occasion, and too much credit cannot be awarded her and her able assistants. ... I failed to get their names ... We realized nearly $100 from the concert. Wilmington, Delaware.

articles.headline: Camden, New Jersey (quarterly meeting in Brother Boyer's charge)
articles.summary: Last Sunday, upon the invitation of Brother Boyer, we attended the quarterly meeting in his charge. We were highly pleased to learn that the very best feeling exists between pastor and congregation, and that their prospects for the future are bright and hopeful.

articles.headline: 1000 Cash Subscribers for Philadelphia: an appeal to the Citizens of Philadelphia in behalf of this paper
articles.author: Elisha Weaver
articles.summary: Fellow Citizens and friends of the oppressed: one more issue after this will settle the question as to whether this paper, for five years, has been efficiently carried on by your humble servant. ... We want one thousand CASH Subscribers in Philadelphia by the first or tenth of January, 1866. ... As soon as we can get into our new building ... we intend to commence to teach our young men the printing business. The prejudices of the owners of printing establishments have been so great, that no colored men were allowed to learn the art of printing. ... We hope all the class-leaders of our Church in this city will take hold of this matter.

articles.headline: Congratulatory Address of Rev. John E. Price, President of the Garnet Equal Rights League
articles.author: Alex. T. Harris
articles.summary: Congratulatory Address of the Rev. John E. Price, President of the 'Garnet Equal Rights League,' delivered on the evening of the 6th [VERIFY] of December, 1865. Ladies and Gentlemen of the Garnet League: A little less than four months ago, you met together, and under the most discouraging circumstances organized this League. ... you have grown from a handful to the number of two hundred and twenty members; comprising some of the most wealthy, intelligent and respectable citizens of this city ... In point of numbers, you are now the Banner League of the old Keystone State. (Continued on p. 3, col. 1, and signed there 'Alex. T. Harris'.) The Garnet League is the HARRISBURG auxiliary (see the Dec 30 'Letter from Harrisburg'), so no names are linked.

articles.headline: A Jolly Time in Philadelphia (church fairs)
articles.summary: The most of our people are having a jolly time in our city, in holding fairs and festivals. Wesley Church, Hurst St., of which Rev. Jacob Mitchell is pastor, has been holding a fair for over a week, and the house has been greatly crowded. The ladies of St. Thomas' Church, of which Rev. Mr. Alston is pastor, have also been at work for several nights. Wesley Church, Lombard St., of which Rev. Mr. Hemer is pastor, is also holding a fair in their church. Little Pine, or Minster St. Baptist Church, has been, and is still holding a fair, and doing very well. Union Bethel Church, of which Rev. J. P. Gibbs is pastor, is also holding a fair for organ for church. Hence, you see we are having a gay time in the city of Brotherly Love.
people: pastor, Union Bethel Church (Rev.; printed J. P.)

articles.headline: The Closing Number of Volume Fifth, 1865
articles.author: Elisha Weaver
articles.summary: The present number completes the Fifth Volume of the Christian Recorder, which commenced its career on the first day of January, 1860, making full five years since we assumed the management of so great a cause as that in which we are now engaged. ... remains a mystery to our own mind how we have regularly issued the paper, beside the superintendence of our Book Depository, the publishing of Hymn-books, Disciplines, Love-feast tickets, &c. Signed 'The Editor'.

articles.headline: Letter from Peekskill (the Philadelphia Tent and the Sarah Tent of New York)
articles.author: Elizabeth Doffels
articles.summary: Mr. Editor: I take pleasure in informing you that I noticed in the Christian Recorder, a few weeks ago, an article which drew my attention, in regard to the separation of the Philadelphia Tent from the Sarah Tent of New York. It is doubtful to me if they were ever united. I was surprised when I heard of them declaring their independence, on account of the neglect of Sister Martha Tow. ... Philadelphia sent five delegates to the city of New York, on July 1st, 1864 ... to confer the degrees upon Rebecca Tent, of Philadelphia; but, as yet, they have never sent for me. Elizabeth Doffels (printed also 'Duffels'), M. of M. J. D. J. U., Peekskill, West Chester Co., New York.

events.name: Odd Fellows' celebration and procession at Baltimore (seventh anniversary of the Order), with the Philadelphia lodges
events.location: Baltimore: Mount Vernon Square, Charles, Madison and Calvert streets; Douglass Hall, Lexington St.
events.description: The editor (E. Weaver) went down on the night line of Oct. 5 with over two hundred colored ladies and gentlemen and over two hundred Odd Fellows from Philadelphia. The Order formed in rank at the depot and marched to Douglass Hall, Lexington street. At 10 A. M. on Oct. 6 the procession formed at Mount Vernon Square, right wing on Madison street, and marched along Charles to Madison street headed by a platoon of the city policemen; 'without the slightest molestation from any quarter'. Chief Marshal of the Day, P. N. F. Greenbury D. Martin; aids P. G. M. C. L. J. Lee and J. Scott; Boyer's celebrated band of some twenty performers; Saml. W. Chase Jr., marshal, aids John H. Griffin and James H. Jordan. Order of the lodges: Nehemiah Lodge No. 1210 (36, marshal James Jackson); Second Manasseh Lodge No. 1214 (35, marshal Isadore Oliver); King David Lodge (23, marshal C. Dutton); Mount Lebanon Lodge (47, marshal Alexander W. Cottman); Zerubbabel Lodge No. 1187 (38, marshal J. C. Hamer); Crystal Fount Lodge No. 100 (48, marshal Elwood Fosgood [?]); Olive Lodge No. 987 (40, marshal Joseph S. Chase); Eden Lodge No. 902 (20, marshal W. H. Brown); a car drawn by eight horses carrying seventeen orphan children under the care of the Grand Lodge; George A. Hackett, marshal and guide; the Mozart Brass Band of Washington (Joseph Anbrush [?], leader; Prof. A. T. Lillie instructor); John F. Cook Lodge of Washington (18); Eastern Star and Potomac Lodge No. 1023 of Alexandria (23); Union Friendship Lodge No. 891 of Washington (25); the Delmonico Band of Philadelphia, Jacob Boyer [?] leader; Wm. Gibson, marshal, with aids J. D. Kelly and James W. Brown; Star of Bethlehem Lodge No. 897 of Wilmington, Del. (27); CARTHAGINIAN LODGE No. 1060 OF PHILADELPHIA (21 members); UNITY LODGE No. 711 OF PHILADELPHIA (26 members). Delegations also from the Good Samaritan, Phoenix, Covenant, Friendship, Mount Olive, Mount Lebanon, Fraternal and Good Hope [lodges] of West Philadelphia [the printed list does not make clear which are of Philadelphia], Good Will of Norristown, United Brethren of Wilmington; the Past Noble Fathers (65) and Council No. 5 of Wilmington (55); then the Grand Lodge of the G. U. O. of O. F. with the Ark and emblems; Grand Master James McC. Crummel of Philadelphia with the Deputy Grand Master, Grand Treasurer and Grand Secretary in three barouches. At Mount Vernon Square, before the court house, exercises opened by Rev. William H. Brown, member of the Order and Past Grand Master, with Grand Master J. McC. Crummel presiding; addresses by Rev. Samuel Chase, Patrick H. Reason of New York (brother of Prof. Reason of the High School) and N. F. James H. Jordan of Baltimore; about nineteen hundred present; procession re-formed at 3 P. M. and returned to Douglass Hall; grand supper at night. The editor also met Bishop Daniel A. Payne at Rev. S. L. Hammond's, with Revs. D. Moore, Hebbard [?], Chaplains Turner and Hall [?] and J. M. Brown; visited the True Communicator (Cooke and Williams, editors) and Rev. W. D. W. Schureman's new Gothic church (40 by ? feet) and parsonage; on Sunday Oct. 8 heard Rev. Mr. Mars at Sharp St. (M. E.) and preached at Bethel, Baltimore; Payne preached at Bethel in the morning and John M. Brown at night. Weaver and Payne returned on Monday Oct. 9.

Military and civic societies assembled on State street at 9 o'clock; line in motion by 10. Order of procession: Chief Marshal; Aids; Drum Corps of the 24th U.S.C.T.; Military, with arms; carriage drawn by four horses containing the Orator of the Day, Wm. H. Day, A.M.; carriage containing Presidents of several Equal Rights Leagues; carriages containing other officers; Delmonico Band; Paxton Lodge of Masons, in full regalia; colored citizens on foot. Owing to some misunderstanding a number of troops at Philadelphia were detained until too late to reach Harrisburg to form part of the procession. The procession halted before the residence of Hon. Simon Cameron, who spoke; calls for General Kiddoo, who acknowledged the compliment. At the Capitol grounds T. Morris Chester introduced Rev. J. Walker Jackson, who prayed; music 'America' by the band; Chester introduced as President Rev. Stephen Smith; Dr. J. H. Smith read resolutions (thanks to the colored soldiers; appeal to undo the 1838 constitutional amendment that deprived colored freemen of Pennsylvania of the franchise; opposition to colonization), which were adopted. Band played 'Tramp, tramp'; Prof. Wm. Howard Day of New York delivered the address. Procession re-formed and marched to the Soldier's Rest for a free dinner. Evening public meetings under the auspices of the State Equal Rights League: at the Court House, Dr. Smith, Mr. Matthews of Baltimore and Prof. Day; at the Wesleyan Union Church, Messrs. J. C. White, Jr., and O. V. Catto. No interference reported. Marshals are not named. || From the Christian Recorder of December 23, 1865, page 2: Mentioned in the Garnet League address: 'On the 14th of November last, you succeeded in giving to the colored soldiers of this State, a reception worthy of their heroic deeds and undying valor.' This is the Harrisburg reception (grand review) of the colored soldiers of the State; Philadelphia participants, if any, are not named in these issues.

events.name: Union A.M.E. Church, Coates St.: all-day services and debt jubilee, Oct. 29, 1865
events.location: Union A. M. E. Church, Coates St., Philadelphia
events.description: General invitation to special sermons throughout the day, Sabbath Oct. 29; speakers engaged: Bishop Wayman (printed 'Weymen'), Revs. W. Moore, W. D. W. Schureman, N. H. Turpin, D. P. Seaton, J. Hamilton and others; a large collection hoped for. Signed by the Elder, Richard P. G[?] (surname uncertain). Bishop Wayman's own appointment list (Oct 21) placed him at Union Church that afternoon after a dedication at Deep Cut, Camden. || From the Christian Recorder of November 4, 1865, page 2: Some three or four weeks earlier the pastor, Elder Gibbs (initials printed 'R. F.' or similar, not legible), announced that he wished to raise $325 on Sabbath Oct. [2]9th and invited Bishop A. W. Wayman, Revs. Moore, Schureman and others. 'Last Sabbath' Rev. Wm. Moore preached in the morning, Rev. W. D. W. Schureman in the afternoon, and Rev. S. D. Flankenburg [VERIFY] of the M.E. Church in the evening; collections through the day amounted to $517.86 [VERIFY figures], more than enough to pay the outstanding debts. The Sabbath school, through Miss Wears, donated $11. Date is 'last Sabbath' before Nov. 4, i.e. Oct. 29; the printed day in the announcement is blurred. || From the Christian Recorder of November 11, 1865, page 1: Reported by the pastor R. F. Gibbs (letter dated Nov. 7) and by 'A Trustee'. Gibbs, appointed June 19, 1865 (transferred from the New York District in July), found about $350 against the church and set Oct. 29 to raise $325. Elder [Wm.] Moore preached in the morning, Elder Schureman in the afternoon, and a white clergyman at night; Bishop Wayman announced $616.59 raised, the largest amount ever raised at one time in Union Church. The jubilee began Monday night [Oct. 30]: Bishop Wayman preached the jubilee sermon, followed by Elder Moore; Messrs. Wm. Davis, Fred. H. Evans (Frederick H. Evans in Gibbs's letter) and Henry Robertson presented a handsomely bound Bible to the pastor, the presentation speech by Wm. Davis. On Sunday afternoon the Sunday school presented $11; the 'Lone Star' association of young men $16 (Gibbs's letter says seventeen dollars); the young ladies' 'Fair Committee' $10. Gibbs's letter gives the church street as Coates St. [VERIFY]. The Nov. 4 issue's figure of $517.86 is superseded by $616.59 here.

events.name: Corner-stone of a new church at Media laid
events.description: Bishop Wayman laid the corner-stone of a new church at Media on Friday, assisted by Rev. Daniel George of the M.E. Church. Reported by 'V.'.

events.name: S. Morgan Smith's reading at Concert Hall
events.description: Although little publicity was given, quite an audience of the elite greeted S. Morgan Smith on Wednesday evening last for his reading of selections from the poets and Shakespeare's soliloquies; Poe's Raven was the gem of the evening.

events.name: Pennsylvania State Equal Rights League, special meeting and public meeting at Harrisburg (called)
events.description: Special meeting of the Pennsylvania State Equal Rights League, Monday evening Nov. 13, 1865, and a public meeting on the evening of the 14th to lay the claims of the Equal Rights movement before the people of Pennsylvania, timed with the Harrisburg reception of colored soldiers. Called by order of the Executive Board: William Nesbit, President; Jacob C. White and Charles B. Colly, Secretaries. Dated Philadelphia, Nov. 7th, 1865.

events.name: Pennsylvania State Equal Rights League: annual meeting at Harrisburg, Aug. 9-10, 1865 (proceedings continued, Nov.-Dec. 1865)
events.description: Continuation of the proceedings (first part printed Sept. 2, in the database). Morning session, President [John] Peck in the chair. Rev. Theodore Green elected a corresponding member on motion of Mr. D. Williams of Hollidaysburg. Report of the Executive Board adopted on motion of Mr. Brown of Hollidaysburg: in the city of Philadelphia six auxiliary leagues formed; seventeen organizations identified with the League by payment of the representation fee; two memorials printed and sent to the State Legislature, one on equal privileges on railroad cars and the other on the elective franchise; numerous public meetings in Philadelphia; a State Convention held at Harrisburg in February; the Solicitor instructed to issue circulars to churches, lodges and other organizations; at a recent meeting of the Philadelphia members committees were appointed for the several districts to hold public meetings. AUXILIARY ASSOCIATIONS REPRESENTED: No. 1, Colored People's Union League Association of Philadelphia, four representatives, Jan. 3d, 1865, $25: John C. Bowers, Stephen Purnell [VERIFY], Jesse E. Glasgow, Rev. John H. Colbert [VERIFY]. No. 2, Equal Rights' League of Sixth District of Phila., one representative, Jan. 27th, 1865, $10: Nathaniel W. Depee. No. 3, John Brown E. R. League of Fifth District of Phila., two representatives, Jan. 30th, 1865, $15 (names not printed). No. 4, Ladies' Union Association of Phila., one representative, Feb. 7th, 1865, $10: William D. Forten. No. 5, Douglass E. R. League, Third District of Phila., two representatives, Feb. 11th, 1865, $15: Rev. David Tilghman, Isaiah C. Wears; alternates, Dr. J. McC. Crummill [VERIFY], Geo. B. White [VERIFY]. No. 6, Ladies' Union Association of Harrisburg: Mrs. Anna E. Amos [VERIFY], Miss Mary Williams alternate. No. 7, Reading E. R. League No. 1, Berks county: Henry B. Fry. No. 8, Friendship Lodge No. 896, G. U. O. of O. F., Phila., one representative, July 31st, 1865, $10: George Whittaker [VERIFY]; Rev. R. Fauset [VERIFY], alternate. No. 9, Lincoln E. R. League, First District of Phila., one representative, August 1st, 1865, $10: Henderson Davis, Jr. No. 10, Rising Sun E. R. League, Second District of Phila., one representative, August 8th, 1865, $10: Lorenzo D. Blackston. No. 11, New Castle E. R. League, Lawrence county: Charles W. Nighten [VERIFY]. No. 12, Benevolent E. R. League, Erie: Henry T. Busley [VERIFY]. No. 13, Bellefonte E. R. League: Franklin Johnson. No. 14, Altoona E. R. League: William Nesbit and John Alexander. No. 15, Hollidaysburg E. R. League: Daniel Williams and Moses Brown. No. 16, Huntingdon E. R. League: John G. Chaplin. No. 17, Pittsburgh E. R. League, Allegheny county: Prof. Geo. B. Vashon. Whole number of associations 17, representatives 22, alternates 4, contributed by auxiliaries $205. Exhibit 1: Dr. James H. Wilson, Treas., in account with the League (receipts $251.59; payments to Jan. 31 publishing bill Recorder $22; printing, Crummill; Solicitor; State Agent; meeting committee; A. M. Green, car case, $30; Langston committee; balance July 19 $2.19). Exhibit 2: James Needham, Treas. (from July 19; balance in fund Aug. 1 $53.50). Mr. Lorenzo D. Blackston of Philadelphia submitted rules for the government of the meetings. Mr. Bustill of Philadelphia presented a resolution on circulating the speeches of Hon. Wm. D. Kelley, Wendell Phillips and Frederick Douglass and letters of Elizur Wright and Robert Dale Owen. Mr. Nesbit of Altoona offered four resolutions on the abuse of the freedmen, citizenship, loyalty and the treatment of colored soldiers. Mr. Price of Harrisburg, on colored men who refuse to accommodate persons of their own color in their business places. Mr. Geo. B. White of Philadelphia offered a resolution for one representative from each district League in Philadelphia on the Executive Board. Mr. Solicitor Bustill of Philadelphia requested lists of churches, lodges and associations with P.O. addresses. Nominating committee (one per county, on Mr. Bustill's motion): Daniel Williams of Blair Co., Geo. B. White of Phila. Co., Samuel Molson of Mifflin Co., O. L. C. Hughes of Dauphin Co., Aaron L. Still of Berks Co., Benjamin Wilson of Luzerne Co., Henry T. Busley of Erie Co., Benj. Fulpress of Allegheny Co., Franklin Johnson of Centre Co., Charles W. Nighten of Lawrence Co., John G. Chaplin of Huntingdon Co., Chas. H. Kelly of Lycoming Co. Business Committee chairman Prof. Vashon of Pittsburgh; on motion of Rev. Jos. A. Nelson of Phila. the report was taken up by resolutions. Resolutions adopted include: approval of retaining colored troops; protest to the Secretary of War and Lt. Gen. Grant at cruel treatment of colored soldiers in Texas; instruct the representatives to the National Equal Rights' League to urge reduction of the fifty dollar fee; commend the constitution of the Agricultural, Commercial, Literary, and Beneficial Society of West Philadelphia; any member who refuses to accommodate colored men in his place of business guilty of dereliction; accept the plan of the National Equal Rights' League. Afternoon session, Vice President Nesbit in the chair; prayer by Rev. Jos. A. Nelson. Executive Board to raise $5000 before March 4 next and to appoint assessors for each district, who are to supervise their districts and take note of all cases where colored men are assaulted on the public highways or thrust from rail road cars, and to prosecute such cases in the courts. (To be continued.) Non-Philadelphia names are in the text only. || From the Christian Recorder of November 25, 1865, page 2: Continuation of the proceedings. Mr. Bustill of Philadelphia objected to reading the Lewistown communication. Mr. Forten of Philadelphia moved the resolution of thanks to the Ladies' Union Associations of Philadelphia, Harrisburg and Pittsburgh for their service to sick and wounded soldiers; adopted on motion of Dr. McC. Crummill of Philadelphia. Resolutions submitted severally by Messrs. Forten, Fauset and Crummill of Philadelphia, referred to the Business Committee. Price, of Harrisburg): Rev. events.name: Funeral of Maurice Hall, Bethel Church
events.location: from No. 1043 Lombard street to Bethel Church (Sixth St.); burial Lebanon Cemetery
events.description: Monday Nov. 13, 1865, 10 a.m., from Hall's residence, No. 1043 Lombard street. Cortege: official members of Bethel Church; Rev. Wm. Moore, pastor; the invited clergy; relatives; a vast concourse of friends. Route: up Eleventh street to Spruce, down Spruce to Sixth, thence to the church (11 o'clock). The choir chanted the dirge 'Why do we mourn departed friends'. Rev. R. F. Gibbs of Union Church read the 12th chapter of Ecclesiastes; prayer by Rev. Jacob Mitchell [VERIFY] of Wesley Church; sermon by Rev. Wm. Moore from Rev. 14:13. By request of brother Hall, Revs. S. Smith and Jos. Frisby [VERIFY] assisted; Smith made remarks, followed by Rev. Frisby. The Daughters of Conference and the Dorcas Society of Bethel Church were largely represented, as well as the Aged Home, a delegation from the latter headed by the matron; Maurice Hall was the leading spirit in the establishment of the Aged Home. At 12 1/2 o'clock his remains were borne to Lebanon cemetery. Funeral procession: relevant to the parades topic.

Henry Gordon, adopted unanimously: in Hall's death the church lost one of its main pillars, the class a worthy leader, the Board of Stewards one of its most efficient members, the Sabbath School of Bethel a time-honored friend and one of its principal founders.

events.name: Union Thanksgiving service of the Philadelphia pastors, Bethel Church (appointed)
events.description: In his list of appointments Bishop A. W. Wayman set Thursday morning, Dec. 7th, at 11 o'clock, at Bethel Church, Philadelphia, for a thanksgiving sermon, and asked the pastors of Philadelphia and vicinity, with their congregations, to meet in Bethel Church and hold a union thanksgiving meeting. events.name: Bethel Sabbath School teachers, special meeting on the death of Maurice Hall
events.description: Special meeting of the teachers of Bethel Sabbath School, presided over by the Superintendent, L. R. Seymour; resolutions adopted on the death of Maurice Hall, one of the founders of the school; sympathy with his aged widow and only son.

events.description: About 8:30 p.m. on November 30, 1865, a dozen or more parishioners called at St. Thomas' parsonage with baskets of groceries and presented Mrs. Annie C. events.location: Wesley A.M.E. Church, Hurst Street, Philadelphia
events.description: Announced for the first Sabbath of 1866 (January 7): members and friends to give a portion of their first week's earnings to liquidate the $1,300 debt on the building. Sermons at 10 1/2 A.M. by Rev. R. P. Gibbs; at 3 P.M. by Revs. Wm. Moore and Stephen Smith; at 7 P.M. by Rev. Bishop Wayman and others. Rev. Jacob Mitchell, Elder in charge; John H. Hughes, Steward.

events.name: A.M.E. Book Concern buys house and lot at No. 631 Pine Street
events.description: The trustees of the A.M.E. Book Concern of Philadelphia announce the purchase of a house and lot at No. 631 Pine Street for the Book Concern and the Recorder (then at 619 Pine). First payment made with borrowed money; possession March 1, 1866; $4,000 wanted by April 25, 1866. The ground fronts on two streets and is valued at $3,000; the building is to train young men in printing and young women in book-binding, paper-folding and bookselling. Committee: Elisha Weaver, chairman; S. Smith; G. M. Mitchell; R. P. Gibbs; W. Moore; H. G. Rhodes. Contributions by Adams' Express or P.O. Box 2075 (elsewhere printed 2975), Philadelphia. (Notice runs dec16 to ap25.)

events.name: Welcome-home sermon to the returned colored soldiers, Bethel Church, Dec. 10, 1865
events.location: Bethel Church, Sixth St. above Lombard, Philadelphia
events.description: Sunday, December 10, 1865, 3 p.m.: Elder (Wm.) Moore's address to the returned soldiers; the church was crowded up and down stairs; Rev. Jacob Mitchell followed with an exhortation and the editor (Weaver) spoke to the soldiers at Mitchell's request. The Bethel choir sang, led by Brother Henry Gordoo [VERIFY] (probably Gordon); performers named only as brother Hance[?]... (illegible), sisters Collins and Misses Armstrong. In the morning Rev. John Jenifer, 'our young brother from California', preached at Wesley Church (Rev. Jacob Mitchell, pastor), and in the evening at Bethel. No soldiers or regiments named. || From the Christian Recorder of December 9, 1865, page 3: Sunday afternoon, December 10, 1865, 2:30 p.m.: a welcome home and congratulating sermon to the returned colored soldiers by the pastor, Rev. Wm. Moore, assisted by other ministers (not named); all returned colored soldiers invited.

events.name: Arrest of discharged colored soldiers James Robison and James W. Loney by Harrisburg police
events.description: As told in their signed letter dated Harrisburg, Dec. 5th, 1865: James Robison (in the text 'Robinson'), of the Third Regiment, just discharged, and James W. Loney, of Philadelphia, also a discharged soldier, rebuked a boy of about nine who insulted them; city officers arrested both and put them in the lock-up, where they were 'treated very badly'. The chief of police, Mr. Barrmot [VERIFY], told Loney 'You are nothing but a nigger' and 'We don't want your black character proved in Harrisburg.' Next morning they were brought out for examination; the outcome is not stated. Loney asks 'what the black man has been fighting for.' (Police violence and harassment of returned soldiers; not a streetcar case.)

events.name: Zion A.M.E. Mission Church, Seventh Street: Third Quarterly Meeting
events.location: Zion A.M.E. Mission Church, Seventh Street between Dickerson and Tasker streets, Philadelphia
events.description: Third Quarterly meeting, Sunday, December 24, 1865; expected: Revs. W. Moore, E. Weaver, R. P. Gibbs, J. Mitchell, G. E. Boyer, D. P. Seaton and others. H. J. Rhodes, minister in charge.

events.name: Garnet Equal Rights League (Harrisburg): congratulatory address of its president
events.description: Address by the Rev. John E. Price, President of the Garnet Equal Rights League, delivered on the evening of December 6 [VERIFY: day blurred], 1865, transmitted over the name of Alex. T. Harris. The League was organized a little under four months before (about August 1865) and had 220 members, 'the Banner League of the old Keystone State'. Its record as listed: introduced the reading of essays and pay lectures (25 cts.) in the city; on November 14, 1865 gave 'to the colored soldiers of this State, a reception worthy of their heroic deeds'; defended Wm. Bush, a returned colored soldier, assaulted on the 1?th ult. [day illegible] by a gang of rowdies, beaten and jailed 'because he was a colored man' to await trial before the Court of Quarter Sessions, where the League supplied counsel and won his release and had his assailants held for the next term on a charge of assault with intent to kill; secured from the Public School Board a school in the Fourth Ward. The League met at the Zion church, Harrisburg (Dec 30 issue), so 'this city', the Fourth Ward school and the Court of Quarter Sessions are Harrisburg's (Dauphin County). Price proposes a separate school for girls taught by a competent female teacher paid from League funds, Sabbath-school work and a reading room.

events.name: Assault on Wm. Bush, returned colored soldier, and his jailing (Harrisburg)
events.description: Per the Garnet League address (Dec 23, p. 2): Wm. Bush, a returned colored soldier, was assaulted in November 1865 (the '1?th ult.'; day illegible) by a gang of rowdies, unmercifully beaten, and then thrust into prison 'because he was a colored man', to await trial before the Court of Quarter Sessions. The Garnet Equal Rights League provided counsel and secured his release, and had his assailants prosecuted and held to appear at the next term on a charge of assault with intent to kill. (Mob and police violence at Harrisburg; not a streetcar case. Non-Philadelphia: not linked.)

events.name: Bishop Wayman preaches at Wesley Church, Philadelphia (appointment)
events.description: Bishop A. W. Wayman's appointments list ends: 'Sunday Jan. 7th, Wesley Church, Philada., Pa.' (the day of Wesley's New Year debt offering announced Dec 16), after Sullivan St. and First St. churches in New York and Brooklyn, Hudson City, Albany, Coxsackie, Catskill, Morristown N.J. (Jan 4) and Reading, Pa. (Jan 5). He adds that he has visited all the stations and circuits but two in the Philadelphia and New York Conferences.

events.name: Church fairs and festivals in Philadelphia, holiday season 1865

Jacob Mitchell; over a week, crowded), St. Thomas' Church (the ladies; Rev. Mr. Alston; several nights), Wesley Church, Lombard St. (Rev. Mr. Hemer [VERIFY]), the Little Pine or Minster St. Baptist Church, and Union Bethel Church (Rev. J. P. Gibbs; for an organ).

events.name: Adjourned public meeting of the colored citizens of Philadelphia (third weekly meeting)
events.location: Philadelphia Institute, Lombard St. above Seventh, Philadelphia
events.description: Thursday evening, December 21, 1865; the third of a series of weekly meetings at the same place. Richard H. Gleaves, president, in the chair; prayer by Rev. Stephen Smith; minutes read by the secretary, J. B. Young. The committee of Messrs. D. [E. D.] Bassett, U. B. Vidal and R. H. Gleaves, appointed at a previous meeting to express the sentiments of the colored community on the Thanksgiving Day sermon of Rev. John Chambers, reported resolutions they had printed and read an Evening Bulletin editorial praising them; report approved, committee discharged. The committee to thank Hon. Charles Sumner and Hon. William D. Kelley made a supplemental report with Sumner's letter (Senate Chamber, Dec. 15, 1865) addressed to E. D. Bassett and Isaiah C. Wear, Esqs.: 'This republic must be free; but this cannot be until all men are equal before the law.' Resolutions moved by U. B. Vidal, discussed by the mover, Rev. Stephen Smith, John C. Bowers (printed 'Bonors') and J. E. Glasgow, adopted: that the word 'white' be stricken from the statute book; rejoicing that 'slave' is no longer recognized by American laws. On motion of Perry Mitchell: since the 'Social, Civil and Statistical Association of the Colored People of Pennsylvania' had arranged a public demonstration to celebrate the abolition of slavery, a committee of three (Messrs. Mitchell, Vidal and Thos. Charnock) to convey the meeting's approval and willingness to take part. Publication committee: E. D. Bassett, Rev. Stephen Smith, J. B. Young. Adjourned to Wednesday evening, December 27, 1865, same place.
attendees: spoke on the resolutions (printed 'Bonors'; John C. Bowers per Michiko)

events.name: Social, Civil and Statistical Association of the Colored People of Pennsylvania: planned celebration of the abolition of slavery (announced)
events.description: Reported in the Dec. 21 citizens' meeting: the Social, Civil and Statistical Association of the Colored People of Pennsylvania had 'already made arrangements for a public demonstration for the celebration of the abolition of slavery in our country' (the Thirteenth Amendment); the citizens' meeting named Perry Mitchell, U. B. Vidal and Thos. Charnock to convey its approval and willingness to participate. Date, route and marshals not given in this issue.

events.name: Equal Rights League of Bensalem (auxiliary to the State League): meeting with Philadelphia speakers
events.description: Held 'on Thursday evening last' before the letter of Monday, Dec. 25, 1865, i.e. Thursday, December 21 (computed). Addresses by William D. Forten and Octavius V. Catto, of Philadelphia. Reported by James Fillman, Solicitor of the Bensalem League.

events.location: Zion A.M.E. Mission Church, 7th Street between Dickerson and Tasker Sts., Philadelphia
events.description: Sunday, December 31, 1865, 3 p.m.: special discourse by the pastor, H. J. Rhodes, on 'The Sign of the Times'.
